On this page

Memory & Conventions ​

Saidi's memory is durable, file-based, and boring on purpose: plain markdown you can read, grep, and edit by hand.

Config lives in repos; memory lives in Saidi — never committed to a client repo.

Layout ​

memory/global.md                    → personal memory (local, single-user install)
memory/members/<userId>/global.md   → per-user personal memory (cloud, multi-member)
memory/projects/<name>.md           → per project agent (shared across the org)
memory/agents/<name>.md             → per custom agent (shared across the org)
memory/runs/<id>/                   → per-run thread state and assets

The split is deliberate: global memory is personal — it follows the human, so in cloud each member has their own. Project and agent memory is shared workspace knowledge and stays org-scoped.

Scopes ​

ts
type MemoryScope =
  | { kind: 'global' }
  | { kind: 'project'; name: string }
  | { kind: 'agent'; name: string };
ScopeInjected intoHolds
globalPRIME's prompt (brainMemoryBlock)Who you are, how you work, standing preferences
projectThat project agent's promptPurpose, layout, run/build/test commands, deploy steps, gotchas, and the policy frontmatter
agentThat custom agent's promptDomain knowledge and conventions for that specialty

What belongs in memory ​

Durable and non-obvious. A fact earns its place if it would still be true next month and is not derivable from the code:

  • The exact deploy procedure, and the ports/env it needs.
  • Which of two similarly-named entities handles which job.
  • A decision that was made and why, so it is not relitigated.
  • A correction you had to give twice.

What does not belong: anything the repo already records (structure, git history, CLAUDE.md), or anything that only matters for one conversation.

The remember tool ​

remember(facts) does not append blindly. The curator reads the existing file, works out whether each new fact is new, an update to something already recorded, or a contradiction, and rewrites the section accordingly. Subject matching is concept-based rather than string-based, with a small stopword list so that a shared leading word ("the", "Saidi", "his") is not treated as a conflict signal.

The practical rule: batch every fact from one task into a single remember call, so the curator resolves them against each other in one pass.

Memory in a Run ​

Memory is selected once, before planning, and held stable for the whole run as appliedMemories:

ts
interface AppliedMemory {
  id: string;
  version: number;
  statement: string;
  kind: 'preference' | 'fact' | 'procedure' | 'lesson';
  scope: 'user' | 'project' | 'agent' | 'task-family';
  scopeId?: string;
  confidence: number;
}

Stable-for-the-run matters: a plan written under one set of remembered conventions should not be executed under a different one.

Compaction ​

When a participant's provider session is compacted, its memory block may be squeezed out of the compact summary. The participant is flagged memoryStale, and the next delegation re-sends the block. PRIME has its own version of this: primeNeedsRehydrate makes the next turn carry the full plan — criteria and evidence, not just status — then clears itself. One rich turn, then back to the cheap one.

Conventions ​

Conventions are just memories that describe how to work rather than what is true. They are surfaced back to an agent at the top of a task, and the task's own instructions override them when the two conflict. Recording one is how you stop repeating yourself.
